metadata.title: Why robotics will be the next great investment theme

content.text:
RoboStrategy (BOT) CEO Andrew Kang joins Yahoo Finance to explain why robotics could become the market's next major investment theme. He discusses how advances in artificial intelligence are accelerating the adoption of autonomous machines and why the convergence of AI and robotics may create significant opportunities for investors.
you know, investors, Andrew, they've been very focused on on AI chips, on cloud computing. Why at a high level Andrew should they say believe that robotics does represent the next great investment theme.
Hey Jon. Thanks for having me. So, robotics has always been a dream in sci-fi, right? You'd hear about it and you'd see it in movies, in TV shows, Futurama, Jetsons, etc, but they were never really a thing, right? Intelligence was always the bottleneck to making these robots work. and now we're getting to a place where we're going to be solving that bottleneck given the recent innovations in AI and physical AI. And so, you can imagine a world where we just completely rethink how labor is done.
where previously, you know, it was done through a very, you know, sweat and and tears and and blood done by humans and eventually, right, now it can be done by humans. And so you can kind of think of, you know, robots or humanoid robots, essentially the GPU equivalent of uh, you know, the AI world. And so that is what really excites us about where robotics is heading and where the industry is going and right now, you know, we're very early, but we are at that inflection point where things are really starting to take off.
When you look at the sort of the robotics value chain, Andrew, where do you think are the smartest investment opportunities right now? Like is it humanoids, uh software, you know, uh industrial automation? What do you see?
It's really all of the above just because the industry we see is potentially being so large. You know, humanoids I think are the ones that are the most buzzy and you see them on uh, you know, media around the world and it's really easy to imagine, right? A human, a robot that looks like a human that can do anything a human can do. And for that sake, that's a really big market because you can have a human or a humanoid robot working in the factory, you can have them working in your home,
you can have them working in hospitality, really any industry across the world. Um, and so that is what I would consider one of the biggest markets is the market for humanoid robots. But also not every single job out there or every single task requires a humanoid robot because you can have a task that is stationary. A lot of jobs or a lot of tasks in factories these days are completely stationary, right? It's you don't need somebody to move and it's it it is very repetitive.
It's the same motion over and over and over again and there's a lot of that work that needs to be done around the world in these industrial tasks. And so we're also very, very excited about companies that are building in the industrial robot and cobot space.
Uh you recently led this this funding round Andrew and for a company called Standard Bots. What does that company do in plain English, Andrew? And what convinced you that that was a smart investment?
Yeah, standard bots makes industrial arms and robot and uh cobots and they are the only industrial arm manufacturer of any decent scale in the US. There are other industrial arm manufacturers across the world in say companies uh countries like Japan or or Germany, but those are old school industrial robots and they're not fit for an AI native world where you need the robots to be a lot more precise. You need them to be durable. You need them to have torque sensing ability. Um and that enables the robots to do a lot more things that they previously weren't capable of doing.
One of the most important things that America is focused right on right now is reindustrialization. Bringing factories and manufacturing back to America and to do that, we don't have enough labor. We don't have the the training uh for the industrial workforce and we just don't have enough people. And so to be able to do that, we're going to need a lot of robots and we believe that Sara bot is going to be one of the pillars of the reindustrialization of of America.
Uh and what what also is really interesting about them is that they are completely vertically integrated and so they aren't dependent on a single uh country outside of the US to be able to produce the robots themselves. Uh and and that is really central to, you know, America's goal of achieving uh both supply chain independence, economic independence, and also manufacturing independence.
Andrew, I'm curious what you make of Elon Musk's efforts in this area in robotics and what you think his competitive advantages are.
Yeah, so what's really interesting was the was the IPO of SpaceX, right? Because previously you'd be able to uh, you know, buy into these companies, these large tech companies when they put when public at a billion dollar valuation or a multi-billion dollar valuation. SpaceX IPO close to $2 trillion. And and so there's a lot of innovation going on in the robotics sector. You know, there's a lot going on within Tesla but then also outside of Tesla, which is why we launched Robo strategy to invest in these private companies that are building in the robotics and humanoid robotics space.
Now, going back to, you know, Elon and Tesla and what they're doing in the robotics space, I think no doubt they're going to be a winner and I am very excited about what Optimus uh with the Optimus group is building. At the same time, I don't think it's a winner take all. I think it's going to look a little bit like the automobile industry where you have a few, maybe a dozen really large players and they all fit different segments of the market. You know, you're going to have something that's really high high class, the luxury market, you know, your Lamborghinis and your Ferraris, you're going to have something that's more middle market, uh still luxury, your Mercedes, your BMWs, and then you're going to have something maybe more economy.
But it's a it's a humongous market. I think it's in the trillions uh tens of trillions of dollars and there's going to be a room for a lot of big players in the space that, you know, we're a lot of which we're invested in and excited about.
You know, Andrew, you also saw Open AI. They're chasing Musk now too. Sam Altman, he's all in on robotics. You saw those headlines and reports. I I was just curious what you made of that and what you think Sam Altman and his team bring to the table.
Yeah, so, you know, they are obviously very strong in LLMs. And I know that they've put together a group to work on humanoid robotics. What I would say is building hardware is a completely different challenge than building software and AI and, you know, the physical AI component is really only one fraction of the challenge to build a really successful humanoid robot uh company. You know, as Elon said when he was building Tesla, manufacturing, figuring out high rate manufacturing was a lot harder than the actual design of the of the car and a lot of the other uh development processes that they were building there.
And so I would not under underestimate the dif difficulty of that that some of the other companies in the space are really building towards and building competency in. and really I I think we'll have to see from from Open AI whether they'll be able to pull up the pull off the hardware and manufacturing component of commercializing a humanoid robot. But look, I I would never, I would never doubt Sam Altman.
Finally, Andrew just sort of a maybe a geopolitical question for you. I've had folks come on the show, Andrew and say it's actually uh China that's leading the way right now in modern robotics, not the US. and I was curious if you agreed with that.
I I think it's very nuanced, you know, I think it's not so much the case that look, only one country is going to win in the robotics industry. I think both country countries are going to have tremendous robotics industries. And I think the way you would look at it is you would look at electric vehicles and you would look at phones. Both America and China make great electrical vehicles and also incredible phones. The thing is what makes really great technology doesn't always equate one to one with
large shareholder value. And so the largest companies in the world today, right, that produce phones, produce cars are American companies, Apple and Tesla. They have the ability to command higher margins, higher brand value, um and and that translates into a much much larger business. Uh the Chinese market, what they have there is they have a lot of competition, which breeds a lot of innovation, it breeds lower prices, greater affordability for consumers in, you know, the Chinese market and the markets that the Chinese sell to, but it doesn't always equate to, you know, what's best for shareholders because they really compete each other down to the bone.
And so, you know, I I think there's going to be some really great robots coming out of China, but I don't really investor envy the investors in in that market.
